subtitle: std::<new> — the foundational header for dynamic memory and exception types. restd's role is strategic re-export plus targeted back-ports: operator new / operator delete and their array variants are runtime-provided and cannot be reimplemented portably, so restd ships namespace-consistent aliases for the std types (bad_alloc, nothrow_t, new_handler, etc.) plus back-ports of the C++17 additions (launder, align_val_t, hardware_*_interference_size) to earlier tiers. Two additional back-ports: bad_array_new_length (added to std in C++11) reaches C++98 as a class deriving from std::bad_alloc; get_new_handler (added in C++11) reaches C++98 via a wrapper that shadows the value passed to set_new_handler. The C++20 destroying_delete_t tag reaches C++11+ as a struct + named instance. Placement new itself is a language operator (not a function), so user code that needs it should #include <new> directly — restd does not and cannot reimplement it.
legend_blurb: Per-symbol coverage of the C++ <new> header. Mostly re-export plus C++17/C++20 back-ports. hardware_*_interference_size is constexpr from C++11 (ahead of std's C++17). launder uses __builtin_launder when available; identity-function fallback otherwise (documented best-effort).

symbols.name: bad_alloc
symbols.notes: Using-declaration from std::bad_alloc. Type identity is preserved — catch on std::bad_alloc& catches restd::bad_alloc and vice versa. restd modules throw restd::bad_alloc() to stay in-namespace.

symbols.name: bad_array_new_length
symbols.notes: C++11+: using-declaration from std::bad_array_new_length. C++98: back-port — class deriving from restd::bad_alloc with what() returning 'bad_array_new_length'. The compiler's array-new path cannot automatically throw the C++98 back-port (that's runtime-provided), but user code that explicitly throws bad_array_new_length works portably. RESTD AHEAD OF STD: 13-year back-port to C++98.

symbols.name: nothrow_t / nothrow
symbols.notes: Using-declarations for std::nothrow_t (tag type) and std::nothrow (constant). Used at the call site for the non-throwing operator-new overload: int* p = new (restd::nothrow) int(42).

symbols.name: new_handler / set_new_handler
symbols.notes: typedef new_handler = std::new_handler. set_new_handler delegates to std::set_new_handler and additionally shadows the value in an internal storage location so the C++98 get_new_handler back-port can return it. noexcept on C++11+; throw() pre-C++11.

symbols.name: get_new_handler
symbols.notes: C++11+: pass-through to std::get_new_handler. C++98 back-port: returns the value last passed to restd::set_new_handler (via function-local-static shadow). Caveat: if user code calls std::set_new_handler directly, the back-port will not see the update. NOT thread-safe pre-C++11 — matches the era's overall lack of threading. RESTD AHEAD OF STD: 13-year back-port.

symbols.name: align_val_t
symbols.notes: Strong typedef for an alignment value. C++17+: using std::align_val_t. C++11-C++14: enum class align_val_t : size_t {}. C++98: struct wrapper around size_t with explicit construction (no enum class). The over-aligned operator-new overloads that take align_val_t are NOT shipped — they're runtime-provided when std supports them (C++17+) and nonexistent earlier. restd surfaces the TYPE so user-facing APIs can express alignment as a strong parameter. RESTD AHEAD OF STD: 19-year back-port to C++98; constexpr-constructible from C++11 (ahead of std's C++17).

symbols.name: launder
symbols.notes: Pre-C++17: forwards to __builtin_launder when D_RESTD_HAS_LAUNDER_INTRINSIC == 1 (the safe path). When the intrinsic is unavailable, falls back to identity function — correct for the common case (read after placement-new of same dynamic type), incorrect for the more aggressive replacement patterns that only matter under heavy optimisation. Detection: __has_builtin(__builtin_launder) || (GCC >= 7). Override by predefining D_RESTD_HAS_LAUNDER_INTRINSIC. RESTD AHEAD OF STD: 19-year back-port to C++98 (best-effort without intrinsic).

symbols.name: hardware_destructive_interference_size
symbols.notes: Minimum offset between two objects to avoid false sharing. Platform heuristic: __GCC_DESTRUCTIVE_SIZE if defined; else __APPLE__ && __aarch64__ -> 128 (Apple Silicon performance cores); else 64. User-overridable via D_RESTD_HARDWARE_DESTRUCTIVE_SIZE before #include. RESTD AHEAD OF STD: 19-year back-port; constexpr from C++11 (std waited for C++17). On C++98 ships as static const std::size_t — same compile-time-constant behaviour for integral types.

symbols.name: hardware_constructive_interference_size
symbols.notes: Maximum offset between two objects to promote true sharing. Default 64. User-overridable via D_RESTD_HARDWARE_CONSTRUCTIVE_SIZE. Same constexpr / C++98-static-const tiering as the destructive variant.

symbols.name: destroying_delete_t / destroying_delete
symbols.notes: C++20+: using std::destroying_delete_t / destroying_delete. C++11-C++17: back-port — struct with explicit constexpr default ctor plus named instance (inline constexpr on C++17+; holder-template pattern on C++11-C++14, matching restd::unexpect / restd::in_place). The operator-delete dispatch that triggers destroying-delete behaviour is COMPILER-DRIVEN — the back-port type cannot trigger the actual behaviour on tiers where the compiler doesn't recognise the overload, but user code can still write the signature so it compiles cleanly. RESTD AHEAD OF STD: 9-year back-port.
symbols.failure_reason: Cannot reach C++98 — back-port requires constexpr ctor (C++11 feature) for the named-instance pattern. C++98 user code that needs a destroying-delete sentinel would have to construct it as a runtime-initialised global; not worth the friction since the destroying-delete operator-overload dispatch itself is C++20 compiler magic.

symbols.name: placement new
symbols.notes: Language operator — not a function. #include <new> from any user-code TU brings in the operator new(size_t, void*) overload; restd does not and cannot reimplement it (operator overloads at namespace scope are linker-visible and runtime-provided). Catalogued here for completeness — every restd module that placement-news (any, expected, array's zero-size workaround, optional, variant, ...) relies on the std header.
